title: Show HN: Coral – Open-source gateway where agents write their own tools
author: jcs
summary: Hi HN, I'm James, one of the co-founders of Coral. Coral is an open-source, self-hosted gateway that sits between your agents and the systems they work on. Agents call tools by writing short TypeScript programs that they can save as custom tools to reuse. You can publish custom tools for groups of agents, so your team’s library of tools adapts to your unique systems, data and use cases. Custom tools help agent performance and give more precise units of permission control. Here’s a short demo: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=p0PKOlHLyVI We started on this while building an AI SRE. To investigate an incident, the agent had to connect the dots across an ocean of telemetry data and undocumented relationships across internal and external systems. It took broad permissions, a lot of tokens and it would start from scratch the next time. We built Coral so that the agent remembers the route. Once a task succeeds, the agent writes the steps that worked into a program and saves it as a custom tool. Next time, the agent finds that custom tool in the same search as standard provider tools (e.g. Datadog, Slack), and reuses it. It started with SRE, but we (and our early users) now use Coral for agent work across the org. For our tasks across GitHub, Linear and Slack with Opus 5.5, custom tools help agents work 29% faster, at 31% lower cost (tasks here: https://withcoral.com/docs/examples/custom-tools ). Coral builds on code mode, adding custom tools, policy controls and managed identities. Each program runs in a V8 isolate with no network access or credentials. Coral checks every tool call against workspace policy before attaching credentials and forwarding it to the provider. You can configure each provider to use the caller’s own account, so teammates can share tools without sharing API tokens. (e.g. https://withcoral.com/blog/slackbot-works-better-with-coral ) Coral is written in Rust, and you can run it as a desktop app or as a shared server. The core is Apache 2.0 and has no limits on users, agents or volume. Everything I've described here is in the OSS edition. SAML, SCIM, and org-wide governance features will be available soon under an enterprise licence. We'd love for you to try it and share your feedback. title: How to Clean Any Messy CSV or Excel Export Without Opening Excel (One Evening)
author: Quill Datafix
summary: Every data pipeline I've inherited starts the same way: someone exported a CSV from a tool that shall remain nameless, and the export is a mess. Not a hard mess — a boring one. That's what makes it annoying: you fix the same four things every single time. The four mess types (and the 10-line fix) import pandas as pd df = pd . read_csv ( "messy_export.csv" , dtype = str ) # read as strings first — see gotcha #1 df . columns = ( df . columns . str . strip ( ) . str . lower ( ) . str . replace ( r "\s+" , "_" , regex = True ) ) # headers nobody agrees on df = df . apply ( lambda s : s . str . strip ( ) ) # trailing/leading spaces df = df . drop_duplicates ( ) # the classic for c in ( "date" , "order_date" , "created_at" ) : # whatever your date cols are if c in df . columns : df [ c ] = pd . to_datetime ( df [ c ] , errors = "coerce" , dayfirst = False ) df . to_csv ( "clean.csv" , index = False ) That's 90% of it. The remaining 10% is where the gotchas live. Three gotchas that silently corrupt your data 1. Letting pandas guess types on read. If a column has "1,234" in row 500, pandas decides the whole column is a string — or worse, silently NaNs it. Read everything as dtype=str , clean, then convert deliberately. 2. Mixed date formats in one column. 2026/03/01 vs 01-03-2026 vs Excel's 45560 serial numbers, sometimes in the same column. pd.to_datetime(..., errors="coerce") turns the unparseable ones into NaT — count them before you trust the column: df[c].isna().mean() . If more than a few percent fail, the column has a format war and you need to handle formats explicitly, not guess. 3. Duplicates that aren't duplicates. " Acme " and "Acme" and "ACME" are the same customer to a human and three rows to drop_duplicates() . Normalize the key columns (casefold + collapse spaces) into a helper column, dedupe on that, drop the helper. If you don't code (or don't want to babysit formats) The steps above are exactly what I packaged into the Excel Batch Cleaner — drop in CSV/XLSX/JSON exports, it runs the space-trim, date fixing, dedupe and header normalization in your browser (files never leave your machine), and writes clean files out. No install, no account. Why it's $1: launch pricing while I collect the first honest reviews — the full cleaner, not a trial. title: How I built Bezel Charts: sixteen SVG charts for the web and Python, with zero dependencies
author: Shaz M
summary: I wanted a chart in a GitHub README. Not a screenshot, but a real chart that looked as good as the rest of the page. That small wish turned into Bezel Charts: sixteen chart tiles as web components, a Python package that draws the same charts from pandas, and a Studio where you can build a chart without writing any code. It's free, MIT licensed, and on npm and PyPI. This is how I built it, the decisions behind it, and a couple of things that went wrong along the way. Why I built it I'm a data scientist, so most of my work ends in a chart. And my charts kept landing in places where chart libraries struggle. A README can't run JavaScript. A small dashboard tile doesn't need a heavy library just to draw a sparkline. And a chart from a notebook rarely looks like the chart on the website it ends up on. I'd already built Bezel , a set of clock, calendar and weather tiles as web components. I liked how they felt: add one tag and you get something that looks finished. So I asked a simple question. What if charts worked the same way? That became the rule for the whole project: a chart should look finished the moment you add it. No config objects, no theme setup, no CSS to fight. What makes it different One tag per chart. ``` Charts fill whatever they sit in and redraw when it resizes, so they work in a sidebar, a card grid or a full-width section without extra CSS. With npm, you can load everything or just the charts you use: js import 'bezel-charts/line'; import 'bezel-charts/bars'; And in Python: python import bezel_charts as bc bc.line(df, x="month", y=["sales", "costs"], heading="Sales", prefix="£") bc.spark(df["signups"], heading="Signups").save("docs/signups.svg") How it works under the hood Every chart is a pure function Each chart takes its options and a theme and returns an SVG string. It never touches the page. The custom element is a thin layer on top that handles sizing, themes, tooltips and the keyboard. That one decision paid off again and again. Tests run in Node in seconds. The same code that draws a chart in the browser also exports it as a static SVG. And toSVG() works on a server, so you can generate chart images in a build script. A size budget that CI enforces Every chart file has its own gzip budget, and the build fails if one goes over. It keeps me honest. When I added real dates and log scales to line charts, that file grew from 9.9 kB to 12 kB, and I had to decide whether the feature earned it. Moving shared code around in the same release made the bars-and-line chart smaller. Python that matches byte for byte The Python package is a line-by-line port of the JavaScript renderers. CI generates test fixtures from the JavaScript and checks that Python draws the identical SVG, byte for byte. So a chart in your Jupyter notebook is exactly the chart on your website. I also cared about the numbers matching what data people already trust. Box plot quartiles use the same method as pandas, NumPy and Excel's QUARTILE.INC , so they line up with df.describe() . Accessibility as a feature, not a checkbox Every chart works without a mouse and without seeing it. Arrow keys move between values, and a screen reader hears something like "Tue: 9. 2 of 7". Lines can have their own dash, points their own shape and bars their own pattern, so series stay distinct without relying on colour, even in black and white. Animation respects reduced-motion settings. And because an exported SVG is just an image, the Python package writes alt text for you with chart.alt . Two things that went wrong Versions drifting apart. I keep npm and PyPI on the same version number. For the 1.8.0 release, one package didn't get bumped and I needed a second tag to fix it. Now a test fails if npm, Python, the library and the built files disagree on the version, so it can't happen again. A broken image on npm. After 1.10.0, I renamed the README image. npm resolves relative image paths against the repository, so the published page pointed at a file that no longer existed. The fix was a full URL for the image. The lesson: anything outside your repo keeps what you published, not what you have now. Try the Studio The easiest way to see what it can do is the live Studio . Pick a chart, then import a CSV, Excel or JSON file, or paste cells straight from a spreadsheet. It works out labels, series and units for you, and your files never leave the browser. When you're happy, Copy HTML gives you the code to paste into a page, Save SVG gives you an image for a README, and Copy link shares your exact chart. No data to hand? There are three sample files to try. Where it's got to I started on 26 October 2026 with eight chart types. Just over two weeks and 35 pull requests later, it's at v1.10.1 with sixteen, on npm and PyPI . A nice surprise: someone found my earlier post here on dev.to and listed Bezel Charts on XERJ Corpus Hub. I've also submitted it to the awesome-web-components list. What's next The size budgets and the Python parity stay as hard rules, so every new chart has to earn its kilobytes. Next, I'm planning to submit it to more curated lists, including awesome-dataviz, and to keep shaping it around what people actually use. So I'd love your input. Which chart would you reach for that isn't there yet? Open an issue, or leave a comment below. Repo: github.com/ShazMoghaddam/bezel-charts Studio: shazmoghaddam.github.io/bezel-charts npm: npm install bezel-charts PyPI: pip install bezel-charts If it's useful to you, a star on GitHub really helps. I'm open to roles and collaborations, in the UK and internationally. If you're working on something with data and think I could help, say hello on LinkedIn or through my website . ` Use the copy button on the block. The title and cover image still go in their own fields at the top.

title: Our wallet audit flagged 40 of 40 Polymarket wallets, but missed the approval all 40 had
author: BotCookery
summary: Originally published on BotCookery , free build recipes for AI-built trading and prediction-market bots. Written with AI assistance. Every number below is from real read-only runs on Oct 25, 2026, against public wallets and accounts that aren't ours. Nothing was signed or sent, and we never held a funded bot wallet or sent a revoke. Nothing here is financial advice. Most bot losses that aren't strategy losses are key losses: a private key committed to GitHub, a seed phrase pasted into a chat to "help debug", a forgotten unlimited approval on a wallet that also holds savings. Our Wallet-Key Safety Pack is a prompt you paste into your AI coding tool. It builds four small Python tools, each with unit tests: secret_scan.py : a pre-commit scanner for private keys and seed phrases env_guard.py : an env loader that refuses unsafe key files kill_switch.py : a one-file kill switch every order path checks first wallet_audit.py : a read-only audit of a bot wallet's balance cap, approvals and API wallets, from its public address only On Oct 25 we pasted the Oct 22 version of the prompt into a clean folder, built it, and pointed the tools at real data: the audit at 40 Polymarket wallets taken from the public trades feed and 60 random accounts from the Hyperliquid leaderboard, and the scanner at our own bot repos and logs. The tools ran. They also missed real risks and buried the rest in noise. Here's what broke and how the prompt changed. Bug 1: the audit missed an approval every active wallet had All 40 wallets had an unlimited pUSD allowance and an outcome-token operator approval for the Neg Risk Adapter . The SDK's approval list leaves that contract out, and Polymarket's contracts page says the CLOB still checks it. Many wallets also still had unlimited USDC.e allowances to the exchanges from before pUSD. The old audit checked neither. The fix: the approval list is now the union of three labelled sources: sdk (the SDK's list, 7 pUSD spenders and 10 operator approvals as of Oct 2026), docs (the Neg Risk Adapter) and legacy (USDC.e allowances and operator approvals for the two old exchanges). Every address is cross-checked against Polymarket's contracts page, and anything not on it is labelled "not on docs page" instead of skipped. Bug 2: every working wallet failed A trading bot needs its approvals. The old audit flagged each one, so all 40 wallets exited 1 with 17 flags. A normal approval looked the same as a leftover one. The fix: by default, approvals are listed as "live" and the audit exits 0. A new --retiring flag turns every live approval and active API wallet into a FLAG (exit 1). Run that when you shut a bot down, not while it trades. Bug 3: the revoke advice did nothing for smart wallets All 40 wallets were smart wallets (Polymarket Deposit, Safe or Proxy). The old audit printed raw approve(spender, 0) calldata, which does nothing if you send it from your key: the approvals belong to the smart wallet. The fix: the audit calls eth_getCode . For a smart wallet it says to revoke through the wallet's own flow (Polymarket's approve_erc20(..., amount=0) and approve_erc1155_for_all(..., approved=False) , or the Safe app). It prints raw calldata only for a plain EOA. Bug 4: the Hyperliquid cap ignored spot The audit read only the perp account value. 42 of the 60 accounts held more in spot than in perps. 14 had under $100 in perps but between $129 and $2.05M in spot, so a $100 cap passed all 14. The fix: total = perp accountValue + spot balances (USDC at $1, other tokens at markPx ). Our first rebuild from the fixed prompt then found three bugs of its own on the live Hyperliquid run: Spot prices were zipped against the pair list by position, but the API returns 1,164 price contexts for 347 pairs, in a different order. That priced HYPE at $0.08 instead of $77.06 and valued one account at $2.34 billion. Now contexts are joined by ctx["coin"] == pair["name"] , never by position. Outcome-token balances ( +36001 ) have no token field and crashed one audit. Now it's b.get("token") , and unpriced tokens are listed. That crash exited 1, the same code as a normal flag. Now any RPC or API error exits 2, so a broken audit can't pass for a flagged or a clean one. Bug 5: the scanner missed most real seed-phrase shapes It caught a 12-word phrase on one lowercase line. It missed a JSON list, a Python list, a numbered list, Title Case, comma-separated words and one word per line, which is how seeds are usually stored. The fix: tokenize the whole file into lowercased letter runs and flag 12+ consecutive BIP39 words when only spaces, newlines, commas, quotes, brackets or "1." numbering sit between them. A ":" or "=" breaks the run, so JSON logs full of common words don't trip it. Bug 6: the scanner drowned in false alarms It raised 100,331 hits on our Polymarket WebSocket logs, from tx hashes and condition IDs. It also flagged .env.example , API_SECRET=... placeholders, "Secrets:" prose, *_KEY_PATH variables and .pyc files. The fix: don't flag a 64-hex value when a hash or ID label sits just before it ( hash , tx , conditionId , order_id and so on). Assignments need a real literal of 8+ characters, names ending in _path , _file , _dir or _url are skipped, placeholders are skipped, binary files are skipped, and .env.example , .env.sample and .env.template are allowed. Bug 7: the hook let a staged key through The pre-commit hook scanned the working copy. In a scratch repo we staged a file with a key, then blanked the file without re-staging. The hook saw a clean file and the key was committed. The fix: with no arguments, the scanner reads the staged content ( git show :<path> for each file from git diff --cached --name-only --diff-filter=ACM ). A new install_hook.py writes the hook with the current Python and refuses to overwrite an existing one. Bug 8: the env guard accepted an empty key It loaded PRIVATE_KEY= (empty) without complaint, and accepted a key file in a world-writable folder. The fix: resolve symlinks first, reject a group- or other-writable parent directory, and treat an empty required value as missing. What the rebuilt version showed We ran the 40-wallet Polygon audit twice, at 2:53 and 2:57 PM ET, and got identical counts both times. All 40 are smart wallets, and 40 of 40 have the Neg Risk Adapter live. Across the 40 there are 42 unlimited legacy USDC.e allowances and 26 legacy operator approvals, and 23 wallets hold more than $100. By default every wallet exits 0. With --retiring , each shows 8 to 24 flags. One wallet's output (wallet address removed): wallet 0x...: smart wallet (Polymarket Deposit, Safe or Proxy) POL 0.0000 pUSD 6,374.39 USDC.e 0.00 FLAG $6,374.39 in stablecoins is above the $100.00 cap: move the excess out checking 24 approvals (17 sdk, 2 docs, 5 legacy) live pUSD allowance -> 0xd91E80cF2E7be2e162c6513ceD06f1dD0dA35296 [docs]: UNLIMITED live USDC.e allowance -> 0x4bFb41d5B3570DeFd03C39a9A4D8dE6Bd8B8982E [legacy] (not on docs page): UNLIMITED live CTF operator 0xC5d563A36AE78145C45a50134d48A1215220f80a [legacy] (not on docs page): approved ... 23 live approvals, 1 not set This is a smart wallet: a plain transaction from your key will not touch these approvals. Revoke through the wallet itself: ... The addresses that remain are Polymarket's own contracts: the Neg Risk Adapter, the old CTF Exchange and the old Neg Risk CTF Exchange. A fresh unfunded address showed "plain EOA", 0 live approvals out of 24 checked, and exit 0. On Hyperliquid, with --cap 100 , 32 of the 60 accounts were flagged and none errored. The 32 include all 14 that had been hiding money in spot. The audit listed 36 API wallets and found none expired. One account (API wallet address removed): perp account value $0.00 spot $182,128.18 total $182,128.18 FLAG total $182,128.18 is above the $100.00 cap: move the excess out 1 API wallet(s) active 'Astro' 0x... valid until 2026-12-02 UTC The scanner now catches 11 of 11 secret shapes and gives 0 hits on our logs and repos: 69 files and 109,213 lines of WebSocket logs, the Hyperliquid starter, and the site's source. In the scratch repo, the hook blocked a key that was staged but deleted from the working file, and it let .env.example through. The 41 offline tests pass. How to use it Nothing in the pack trades, signs or sends. The audit takes a public address and refuses anything shaped like a private key. So it's safe to run on day one, before you build any bot: Paste the prompt into your AI coding tool in a new wallet-guard folder, then run the tests offline first. Install the scanner as a pre-commit hook in every bot repo with install_hook.py , then prove it: stage a throwaway 64-hex string and watch the commit get blocked. Before you paste text into an AI tool, pipe it through secret_scan.py --stdin . Move the bot's key file to ~/.config/<bot>/.env , chmod 600 , outside the repo, and load it with env_guard.load_secrets(...) . Put kill_switch.check() at the top of every order path. Practise on a fresh throwaway address with no funds: audit it (expect zero balance and no approvals), turn the kill switch on and confirm your paper bot refuses orders. When a bot retires, run the audit with --retiring , revoke everything it lists through your own wallet, and move the balance out. The audit prints what to revoke; it never does it for you. Exit 1 means a flag. Exit 2 means the audit couldn't finish, so don't read it as clean. And the rule the tools can't enforce: never paste a seed phrase or private key into an AI chat, an issue or a screenshot. Your AI coding tool only needs the name of the environment variable your code reads. What we tested, and what we didn't The page's verified line, word for word: Verified working on live data in read-only mode, Oct 25, 2026. Audits ran live, read-only, against 40 active Polymarket wallets, 60 Hyperliquid leaderboard accounts and a fresh unfunded address. None of them is ours, and we never held a funded bot wallet or sent a revoke. The scanner and hook ran on our own repos and a scratch repo with throwaway keys. So: the audit's reads were checked on live data, and the revoke paths were not exercised. Revoking is something you do yourself, in your own wallet. The full recipe, with the complete prompt, a follow-up prompt for builds made before Oct 25, step-by-step setup, the safety checklist and links to the Polymarket and Hyperliquid docs behind it, is at botcookery.com/recipes/wallet-key-safety-pack .

title: Publishing Pipeline Scheduled vs Immediate
author: Francis Oyakhire
summary: This week’s news about AI model inference and deployment strategies has sparked a broader conversation about control, cost, and complexity in modern software stacks. As we look at the tradeoffs between scheduled and immediate publishing pipelines, we find a similar tension: when do we let the system decide, and when do we take the wheel? At Apex Grid, we’ve built a hybrid approach that balances the need for timely content delivery with the flexibility of scheduling - and it’s not without its challenges. We run a platform that handles both immediate publishing - like real-time analytics dashboards - and scheduled content - such as social media posts and long-form articles. For the latter, we needed a way to publish content at a specific time, but also ensure that the content remains consistent across all platforms. That’s where the canonical URL problem comes in. When a post is scheduled, it’s stored in a draft state, and only published when the cron job fires. However, if a user shares a preview link to the draft before it’s published, that link becomes invalid once the post goes live. This creates a mismatch between the canonical URL (which is the final, published version) and the URL used in the preview. To solve this, we implemented a redirect system that maps draft URLs to their published counterparts once the post is live. Here’s a simplified version of how we handle the redirect in our backend: from flask import Flask , redirect , request import re app = Flask ( __name__ ) # In-memory mapping of draft URLs to published URLs draft_to_published = { "/drafts/2026-04-05-hello-world" : "/posts/2026-04-05-hello-world" , # ... more mappings } @app . before_request def handle_redirects ( ) : path = request . path if path in draft_to_published : return redirect ( draft_to_published [ path ] , code = 301 ) This approach works well for small-scale use cases, but it has limitations. The in-memory mapping is not scalable and doesn’t handle edge cases like deleted posts or posts that are moved. To address this, we’re moving toward a more robust solution that uses a database to store and manage the canonical URL mappings. This will allow us to query and update mappings dynamically, and also add features like soft-deletes and versioning. The tradeoffs are clear. Using a database adds complexity and latency, but it also provides consistency and reliability. We’ve found that the benefits of a centralized, scalable system outweigh the costs, especially as our platform grows and the number of scheduled posts increases. Looking ahead, we’re exploring ways to automate the canonical URL mapping process. One idea is to generate the canonical URL based on the post’s metadata, such as the title and publication date. This would reduce the need for manual mappings and make the system more self-sufficient. We’re also considering integrating with reverse proxies to handle redirects at the network level, which could improve performance and reduce the load on our application servers. What do you think about the tradeoffs between manual and automated canonical URL mapping? And how would you handle the problem if you were building a hybrid publishing pipeline for a global audience?

title: Inventory Sync Before Black Friday: 5 Edge Cases Your Tests Miss
author: API2CartOfficial
summary: Last Black Friday, US shoppers spent $11.8 billion online in a single day, according to Adobe Analytics. That's roughly $8.2 million per minute, on average across the day. Every order changes a stock number somewhere. If you build order management, inventory management or multichannel software, your synchronization logic probably works fine on a normal Tuesday. Peak traffic is different. It doesn't necessarily create new bugs. It exposes edge cases that never appeared in testing. TL;DR: calculate stock buffers for fast-selling products, sync every relevant order status change, keep unpaid and returned stock separate, and never rely on webhooks alone. Process events idempotently and run scheduled reconciliation. Here are five edge cases, why they matter, how to handle them and how to test your implementation before Black Friday. The code is a Python sketch of the pattern, not a ready-made client. 1. Two channels can sell the last unit before your next sync Shopify sells the last hoodie at 09:00:04. Amazon sells the same hoodie at 09:00:31. Your inventory sync runs every five minutes, so both channels still show one unit available. Now you have two orders and one item. On Amazon, this has a direct consequence: sellers must keep their cancellation rate below 2.5%. The metric covers seller-fulfilled orders that the seller cancels before shipping, measured over a seven-day period, so cancelling because of insufficient stock pushes it up. You cannot make synchronization instantaneous, but you can reduce the quantity exposed on each marketplace. A common starting point is a buffer for fast-moving SKUs. Instead of always holding back two units, estimate the buffer from sales velocity and synchronization delay. In the sketch below, sales_per_hour is a simplified assumption: the same sales rate on each of the other channels. import math def marketplace_quantity ( on_hand , sales_per_hour , sync_lag_minutes , other_channels , max_buffer = 5 ) : """Estimate units to hold back against sales on other channels. sales_per_hour: assumed rate on EACH other channel.""" expected_elsewhere = ( sales_per_hour * ( sync_lag_minutes / 60 ) * other_channels ) buffer = min ( math . ceil ( expected_elsewhere ) , max_buffer ) return max ( on_hand - buffer , 0 ) marketplace_quantity ( 12 , sales_per_hour = 6 , sync_lag_minutes = 5 , other_channels = 1 ) # 11 marketplace_quantity ( 12 , sales_per_hour = 30 , sync_lag_minutes = 15 , other_channels = 2 ) # 7 ⚠️ This is a simplified heuristic, not a universal inventory formula. Real buffer calculations should account for channel-specific sales rates, shared inventory, fulfillment rules and the possibility of simultaneous orders. A buffer reduces the risk of overselling; it doesn't guarantee that concurrent orders can't exceed available stock. The cap also matters. Without one, a slow sync on a fast-selling product could hide most of your available stock. Recalculate sales velocity from recent data rather than last month's average. During Black Friday, yesterday's sales rate may be more useful than last month's. 🧪 Test it: sell the same SKU on two channels within one synchronization interval. Check whether the buffer would have prevented the oversell. 2. Cancellations and refunds must reach every channel A sale reduces stock, and your connector pushes the updated quantity to every marketplace. Then the customer cancels. Stock returns to your store, but nothing happens on the other channels. Some integrations process new orders correctly but fail to propagate later order status changes. The result is inventory that is physically available but still invisible on Amazon, eBay or another marketplace. Two design choices help prevent this: Treat inventory changes as a signal to refresh a SKU. Whether the trigger is a new order, a cancellation, a refund with restocking or a manual adjustment, retrieve the current available quantity from your source of truth and update the relevant channels. Schedule a full inventory sync. If an event is missed, the next reconciliation can correct the discrepancy. There is an important distinction between refunds and cancellations. A refund does not necessarily restore inventory. The result depends on the platform and on whether the item was actually restocked. Always read the resulting inventory quantity instead of assuming that every refund adds one unit back. 🧪 Test it: place an order, cancel it and check the marketplace listing. Repeat the test with a refund, and check whether the item was actually restocked, not just refunded. Verify that the correct quantity reaches every channel exactly once. 3. Unpaid orders can reduce stock across every channel In WooCommerce, an order with the On hold status, such as one waiting for a bank transfer, already reduces stock. If payment is confirmed, the stock remains reduced. If the order is cancelled, WooCommerce restores it. This is reasonable within a single store. But if WooCommerce is your source of truth, that lower quantity may be pushed to every connected marketplace. One customer who never pays can temporarily hide your last available units everywhere, precisely when demand is highest. Your inventory logic should explicitly define: Which order statuses count as committed stock. You may want to treat On hold units as unavailable in the store while handling them differently in your multichannel inventory logic. How long unpaid orders remain active. If your business rules allow it, implement a separate cleanup for stale On hold orders created by manual-payment methods. Don't assume WooCommerce's built-in Hold stock timer handles them: that setting applies to eligible Pending payment orders, not to On hold. How cancellations propagate. Once an order is cancelled and stock is restored, the updated quantity must reach every connected channel. The key is to distinguish physical stock from stock reserved by active orders. 🧪 Test it: create a bank-transfer order in WooCommerce and leave it On hold. Check the quantity on every connected marketplace. Then cancel the order and confirm that the units become available again. 4. Fulfillment locations and returns belong to separate inventory pools A single stock number per SKU stops working as soon as inventory is held in more than one place. Consider a seller using both their own warehouse and Amazon FBA. FBA stock is stored and shipped by Amazon. It should not be mixed with the seller's own warehouse quantity. Returns introduce another distinction. Amazon evaluates returned FBA items as either: Sellable: the item can return to available inventory. Unsellable: the item cannot be offered for sale as available stock. A return that is still being processed is not inventory you can ship. If your synchronization logic adds every return directly to available stock, you risk selling units that are not ready to fulfill. Model inventory pools explicitly: POOLS = { "own_warehouse" : { "sellable" : True , "channels" : { "shopify" , "ebay" , "amazon_mfn" } } , "returns_pending" : { "sellable" : False , "channels" : set ( ) } , "amazon_fba" : { "sellable" : True , "channels" : { "amazon_fba" } } } def available_for ( channel , stock_by_pool ) : return sum ( qty for pool , qty in stock_by_pool . items ( ) if POOLS [ pool ] [ "sellable" ] and channel in POOLS [ pool ] [ "channels" ] ) stock = { "own_warehouse" : 10 , "returns_pending" : 3 , "amazon_fba" : 20 } available_for ( "shopify" , stock ) # 10 available_for ( "amazon_fba" , stock ) # 20 ⚠️ The example is a simplified scheme that illustrates the principle: calculate availability from the inventory pools that each channel can actually fulfill from. Real FBA availability has more states (reserved units, inbound shipments and others) that this sketch doesn't model. Move returned units from returns_pending to a sellable pool only after inspection or confirmation from the fulfillment platform. 🧪 Test it: process an FBA return and check where the units appear. Verify that they don't become available before Amazon reports them as sellable. 5. Webhooks get missed, retried and duplicated During a traffic spike, your webhook endpoint can slow down, time out and fail deliveries. Shopify, for example, retries failed webhook deliveries up to eight times over four hours. If all attempts fail, Shopify stops retrying and may remove the webhook subscription, depending on how it was created. Retries also mean that the same event can arrive more than once. Shopify expects your endpoint to respond within five seconds , so acknowledge the event fast and move the real work to a queue. This creates two separate problems: An event may never reach your application. An event may reach your application more than once. Your integration needs to handle both. Make webhook processing idempotent Before anything else, verify the delivery. Shopify signs each webhook with the X-Shopify-Hmac-Sha256 header; check it against the raw request body using Shopify's documented algorithm. Then use X-Shopify-Webhook-Id , which Shopify recommends for detecting duplicate deliveries. The order of operations matters. If you mark a webhook as processed and the application crashes before the job is queued, the retry will be rejected as a duplicate and the change is lost. Saving the delivery record and the job in one database transaction (an inbox and an outbox) avoids that. This example handles Shopify's inventory_levels/update topic. Other webhook topics need their own payload mapping. def handle_inventory_level_webhook ( headers , raw_body , payload , secret , db , verify_shopify_hmac , sku_lookup ) : # Header names may arrive lowercased; use a case-insensitive lookup. h = { k . lower ( ) : v for k , v in headers . items ( ) } if not verify_shopify_hmac ( h . get ( "x-shopify-hmac-sha256" ) , raw_body , secret ) : return "unauthorized" webhook_id = h [ "x-shopify-webhook-id" ] sku = sku_lookup ( payload [ "inventory_item_id" ] , payload [ "location_id" ] ) # Save the delivery and the refresh job together: # either both are stored or neither is. with db . transaction ( ) : if not db . inbox_insert_if_new ( webhook_id ) : return "duplicate" db . outbox_add ( "refresh_sku" , sku = sku , idempotency_key = webhook_id ) return "accepted" # respond fast; a worker processes the outbox verify_shopify_hmac stands for an implementation of Shopify's official verification: compute the HMAC from the raw body and your app secret, and compare it with the supplied value using a constant-time comparison. inbox_insert_if_new stands for an insert protected by a unique constraint, not an in-memory set. Note another detail: inventory webhooks don't necessarily contain the SKU. Shopify's inventory level events, for example, identify the inventory item and the location. Your integration needs a reliable mapping from platform inventory identifiers and locations to its own product records. Most importantly, don't blindly apply the same inventory delta every time a webhook arrives. Use the event as a signal to refresh the current stock state from your source of truth. How you write that quantity back depends on the platform and its concurrency behavior. An absolute update can overwrite a newer change if an older value arrives late. A relative update (increase or reduce by N) avoids overwriting changes made by other systems, but it's unsafe if the same event is applied twice. Use idempotency keys, process updates for one SKU in order, and choose the update method each platform handles best. Also account for event ordering. Shopify doesn't guarantee that webhooks arrive in the order the events occurred; it suggests using the X-Shopify-Triggered-At header or the payload's updated_at to order them. Combined with re-reading the current stock from your source of truth, that keeps stale events from overwriting newer data. Run scheduled reconciliation Even reliable webhook processing can't guarantee that your inventory always matches every marketplace. A reconciliation job compares the expected quantity with what each channel currently shows and corrects the difference. It should count a fix only when the write actually succeeded: def reconcile ( skus , expected_by_channel , channel_quantity , set_channel_quantity , channels , alert , drift_alert_at = 3 ) : fixed , failed = [ ] , [ ] for sku in skus : expected = expected_by_channel ( sku ) for channel in channels : target = expected [ channel ] listed = channel_quantity ( channel , sku ) # None if the read failed if listed is None : # don't guess failed . append ( ( sku , channel , "read_failed" ) ) continue if listed == target : continue # Returns True only when the platform confirms the update. if set_channel_quantity ( channel , sku , target ) : fixed . append ( ( sku , channel , listed , target ) ) if abs ( listed - target ) >= drift_alert_at : alert ( sku , channel , listed , target ) else : failed . append ( ( sku , channel , "write_failed" ) ) return fixed , failed Alert only when the drift is large; otherwise the alerts get ignored within a week. In production, reconciliation also needs pagination, retries for the failed list and rate-limit handling. Never treat an unsuccessful API response as a confirmed inventory value. During peak periods, run reconciliation more often for fast-selling products and less often for the long tail. Keep API rate limits in mind: a full comparison of thousands of SKUs across several channels can generate a lot of requests. 🧪 Test it: stop your webhook endpoint for a few minutes, place an order and restore the endpoint. Verify that reconciliation detects and fixes the difference. Then replay the same webhook twice and confirm that inventory isn't reduced twice. One more thing before the code freeze None of these cases is particularly exotic. They simply happen too rarely during a normal week to show up in everyday tests. Test them now: place an order, cancel it, issue a refund, process a return and temporarily stop your webhook endpoint. Finding a synchronization problem during testing is cheaper than finding it through customer complaints on Black Friday weekend. If you're building inventory synchronization across many platforms, maintaining a separate integration for every marketplace makes this work harder with each one you add. Platform-specific capabilities still matter, but a unified integration layer can simplify the work. See how inventory synchronization works with API2Cart . 🎥 Prefer video? title: When I tell Cursor "just make it work", this rule stops the shortcut from rotting
author: ShipStack
summary: Cursor is very obedient about the word "quick." If I say "just make it work," it will often make something work by skipping the parts that are annoying: the ownership check, the empty state, the test, the rollback. The feature looks done. A week later I cannot remember which of those shortcuts is load-bearing, and one of them is in a path real users hit. I got tired of cleaning that up, so I stopped treating "MVP" as a quality setting. I treat it as a scope setting. The rule lives in .cursor/rules/ and I pull it in when I hear myself say "hack this in," "just for now," or "we'll tidy it later." Cut scope, not quality The useful question is not "how do we write this faster?" It is "what can we not build yet?" I tell the agent to cut these first: A settings screen. A named constant at the top of the file is enough for one flag. An admin panel. A script or a SQL snippet in /scripts will do. Teams and roles. Stay on a single user, but keep userId on every record so you can add teams later without a rewrite. A custom design system. Use the component library already in the repo. Edge-case polish. A clear error message is enough. I also tell it what it is not allowed to cut, even in a hurry: Auth and ownership checks. Input validation at API boundaries. Idempotency for payments and webhooks. Error logging. A console.error with context is better than a silent catch . Types on function signatures that cross a module boundary. That split is the whole point. "Quick" means the settings UI can wait. It does not mean the webhook can be processed twice. Shortcuts have to be greppable Some debt is still worth taking. When I take it, I want to find it again on a Monday morning, not rediscover it in production. I use one comment format: // DEBT(solo): <what's missing> — <when it'll hurt> — <how to fix> // DEBT(solo): no pagination — breaks past ~1k items — add a cursor param to /api/items Three rules around it: The marker has to say what is missing, when it will hurt, and how to fix it. "TODO later" is not a plan. At most three new DEBT(solo) markers in one change. If I need a fourth, the slice is too big and the agent should say so, not keep going. grep -R "DEBT(solo)" is the backlog. If it is not greppable, it does not count. This is boring on purpose. The alternative is a vague "we'll refactor this" that nobody can search for. Prototype and production are different folders If I say "prototype" or "throwaway," I want it in /sandbox or on a separate branch, and I want the agent to say out loud that it is not production-safe. If a real user can reach it, it is production. The "never cut" list applies. Putting a prototype in the same routes as checkout, "just to see," is how a labelled shortcut becomes an unlabelled incident. A compact rule you can paste Save this as .cursor/rules/60-mvp-not-sloppy.mdc . It is not always-on. It should attach when the task is a prototype, a spike, or a deliberately small first version. --- description: "Use when the user says quick, MVP, hack, or just make it work." alwaysApply: false --- # Fast but not sloppy "Quick" means fewer features, not worse code. Cut scope, keep quality. ## Cut these first - Settings/config UI → a named constant at the top of the file. - Admin panels → a script or SQL snippet in /scripts. - Multi-tenant/team support → single user, but keep userId on every record. - A custom design system → the component library already installed. - Edge-case UX polish → a clear error message is enough. ## Never cut these - Auth and ownership checks. - Input validation at API boundaries. - Idempotency for payments and webhooks. - Error logging (a console.error with context beats silence). - Types on function signatures that cross module boundaries. ## Debt you take on must be labelled ```ts // DEBT(solo): <what's missing> — <when it'll hurt> — <how to fix> ``` Max 3 new DEBT markers per change. If you need more, the scope is too big; say so. ## Prototype vs production - If the user says "prototype / throwaway", put it in /sandbox or a separate branch and say it is not production-safe. - Anything reachable by real users is production. Apply all of the above. After that I still ask for a short done-summary: what changed, how to verify, and which DEBT(solo) items were added. If the summary has no debt list and the diff quietly skipped a test, the rule did not run. What this does not replace This is not a substitute for a small-diff rule, a bug-fix playbook, or a real review. It only answers one failure mode: the agent heard "hurry" and lowered the quality bar instead of the feature bar. If you want the rest of the set I use (core working agreement, feature slicing, root-cause bug fixes, PR review, landing copy), I bundled them as a one-time Cursor pack: shipstack.sognia.workers.dev/cursor-pack . The rule above is usable on its own. Free sample rule: https://shipstack.sognia.workers.dev/sample

title: How We Built a Remote 10-Tool Streamable HTTP MCP Server and 13.3 KiB Link-in-Bio in Go
author: Giuliano Ribeiro
summary: Public link-in-bio pages are structurally simple documents: an avatar, a name, a contact bar, and 5 to 20 links. Yet most commercial bio-link platforms render them as client-heavy Single-Page Applications that download hundreds of kilobytes of framework JavaScript inside Instagram, TikTok, or WhatsApp in-app WebViews before painting a button. When we built Linq.es and its Official Remote MCP Server ( https://linq.es/mcp ) , we took the opposite path on both the public frontend and the AI agent layer: Public profiles render server-side in Go ( html/template ) with inline critical CSS, 5.1 KiB of gzipped async CSS, 8.2 KiB of gzipped defer vanilla JS, and zero React, Next.js, or Vue runtime ( 13.3 KiB total gzipped first-party CSS + JS). AI agents connect directly to https://linq.es/mcp over Streamable HTTP ( JSON-RPC 2.0 , MCP spec 2025-03-26 ) using a Personal API Key ( lnq_live_... ), without installing a local npx or Python stdio wrapper. Below are the main architectural lessons we learned building both layers in Go. 1. Why Go HTML SSR beats heavy SPA bundles inside social WebViews Most link-in-bio clicks happen inside constrained mobile WebViews (Instagram, TikTok, LinkedIn, X, and WhatsApp) over variable cellular connections. Every extra script tag, font round-trip, and client hydration pass delays First Contentful Paint and increases bounce rates before a visitor taps a wa.me button or downloads a .vcf contact card. On Linq.es, public profiles render complete semantic HTML in the European Union behind a multi-tier cache (in-memory L1, persistent object storage L2, and Cloudflare Edge CDN): Async stylesheet: ~5.1 KiB gzipped (loaded non-blocking) Deferred vanilla JS: ~8.2 KiB gzipped (loaded with defer) Total external CSS+JS: 13.3 KiB gzipped (zero client SPA framework) No third-party ad pixels (Meta, TikTok, or GA4) are injected on public pages unless a Pro profile owner explicitly configures their own measurement IDs. 2. Streamable HTTP MCP ( 2025-03-26 ) vs local stdio wrappers Many early MCP integrations wrap an existing REST API inside a local Node.js stdio package that users run via npx -y @vendor/mcp-server . That introduces three recurring friction points: Node or Python version mismatches on developer machines Stale local npm packages when tool schemas or annotations evolve No support on cloud, browser, or mobile MCP hosts that cannot spawn local subprocesses With the 2025-03-26 Streamable HTTP specification, an MCP server runs as a standard HTTPS JSON-RPC 2.0 endpoint: GET https://linq.es/mcp serves human-readable discovery metadata ( name: "linqes-mcp" , protocolVersion: "2025-03-26" , transport: "streamable-http" ). POST https://linq.es/mcp handles initialize , notifications/initialized , ping , tools/list , and authenticated tools/call executions. Lesson #1: notifications/initialized must return 202 Accepted with an empty body During the MCP handshake, right after initialize succeeds, strict clients send a JSON-RPC notification ( {"jsonrpc": "2.0", "method": "notifications/initialized"} ) that omits the id field. If your HTTP router wraps every return path in a 200 OK JSON-RPC envelope with "id": null , strict clients treat the unexpected body as a protocol error. In Go + Gin, handling JSON-RPC notifications before dispatching methods keeps the handshake clean: // JSON-RPC notifications omit "id" and must not return a JSON-RPC response body. if strings . HasPrefix ( req . Method , "notifications/" ) || len ( req . ID ) == 0 { c . Status ( http . StatusAccepted ) return } Lesson #2: Evict edge caches synchronously on serverless runtimes On serverless container platforms, CPU allocation drops as soon as the HTTP response finishes writing. If an AI agent calls add_profile_link or update_profile_link and you trigger CDN cache purges in detached background goroutines, the container can be throttled before the outbound purge completes, leaving visitors looking at stale HTML when the agent reports the link is live. Running storage and CDN cache invalidations concurrently inside a sync.WaitGroup before returning the tools/call response guarantees that by the time Claude or Cursor replies "Done, live at https://linq.es/handle" , public visitors already see the updated page: var wg sync . WaitGroup wg . Add ( 2 ) go func ( ) { defer wg . Done ( ) purgeObjectCache ( ctx , profileHandle ) } ( ) go func ( ) { defer wg . Done ( ) purgeEdgeCDN ( ctx , profileHandle ) } ( ) wg . Wait ( ) Lesson #3: Explicit MCP Tool Annotations ( 2025-03-26 ) matter for agent safety When exposing read, write, and delete operations side by side, tool descriptions alone should not force an LLM host to guess which calls are safe to auto-approve and which require human confirmation. Adding standard MCP annotations ( readOnlyHint , destructiveHint , idempotentHint , and openWorldHint ) using explicit boolean pointers in Go ensures false values serialize cleanly instead of being dropped by omitempty : type MCPToolAnnotations struct { Title string `json:"title,omitempty"` ReadOnlyHint * bool `json:"readOnlyHint,omitempty"` DestructiveHint * bool `json:"destructiveHint,omitempty"` IdempotentHint * bool `json:"idempotentHint,omitempty"` OpenWorldHint * bool `json:"openWorldHint,omitempty"` } Combined with "additionalProperties": false on every tool's inputSchema and clear prerequisite notes (e.g., calling list_profiles to discover handles and list_profile_links before update_profile_link or delete_profile_link ), agents avoid hallucinating parameters or accidentally deleting links when a user only asked to hide one ( active: false ). Connecting to https://linq.es/mcp Once you generate a Personal API Key in Account Settings, you can connect Cursor ( ~/.cursor/mcp.json ), Claude Desktop, Windsurf, or Gemini CLI ( ~/.gemini/settings.json ) directly over HTTPS: { "mcpServers" : { "linqes" : { "url" : "https://linq.es/mcp" , "headers" : { "Authorization" : "Bearer lnq_live_YOUR_PERSONAL_API_KEY" } } } } From there, your agent can use all 10 tools across up to 5 profiles and 500 /s/ shortlinks: list_profiles : List owned profiles, themes, public URLs, and cumulative view counts. get_profile_analytics : Pull 1-to-90-day views, clicks, CTR percentage, referrers, countries, devices, and daily time series. list_profile_links : Inspect every link's key , url , active state, click count, and iOS/Android overrides. add_profile_link : Publish a link or social icon with optional badgeText , iosUrl , androidUrl , scheduleStart / scheduleEnd ( RFC3339 ), live countdown, or click badge. update_profile_link & delete_profile_link : Edit, toggle ( active: false ), or permanently remove links with immediate cache invalidation. import_bio_links : Migrate public links from an existing Linktree, Beacons, or Bio.link URL in one call. list_shortlinks & create_shortlink : Create and audit https://linq.es/s/:code shortlinks with custom 3-50 character slugs, iOS/Android routing, and utm_source through utm_content tags. list_leads : Retrieve recent Name, Email, and WhatsApp contacts captured via your profile's Lead Magnet form. You can inspect the live discovery metadata anytime with curl -s https://linq.es/mcp | jq . , try the free .vcf , WhatsApp, and UTM generators without an account at https://linq.es/tools , or read the full MCP setup docs at https://linq.es/integrations/mcp .

title: Un enlace con el nombre correcto también puede terminar en otra página
author: jakhari
summary: En una revisión de código me gustaría que alguien copiara un enlace del pie de página y lo abriera en una pestaña nueva. Puede parecer una tarea aburrida. Sin embargo, el texto del enlace podría decir «ayuda» y la dirección terminar en la portada. Quizá la página haya cambiado de lugar hace poco. También puede pasar que funcione desde un menú y falle desde otro. Es una diferencia difícil de detectar cuando solo se revisa cómo se ve el sitio. Para situar el ejercicio, www.casinoconsejos.com es un ejemplo de un sitio de contenido orientado a Costa Rica. Los fallos que se describen aquí son ejemplos de una maqueta, no hallazgos sobre ese dominio. El objetivo es escribir una comprobación que pueda repetirse en un sitio con muchas categorías y enlaces internos, se trate de una guía de juegos o de cualquier otro archivo editorial. Haz un inventario de rutas prometidas Escoge tres enlaces que tengan un buen objetivo, por ejemplo, «contacto», «privacidad» e «información sobre el cierre de cuenta». Copia la parte que es visible en el enlace y a continuación la dirección que aparece. Después, señala el título de la página que se abre y si el título y el destino hacen referencia a cosas diferentes, ese es un buen indicio para seguir investigando. La dirección que se devuelve puede llevar a una página válida, y, a pesar de eso, puedes ir al lugar equivocado. Respecto a ciertos informes automáticos, la primera objeción que tengo es que una respuesta HTTP 200 la asuman como prueba de que el enlace sirve. En realidad, ese código significa que se ha dado una respuesta correcta a nivel HTTP, pero no dice si ha abierto una ayuda de cuenta, si ha abierto una portada genérica o ha abierto una página relacionada con otra operación. En una revisión pequeña también tengo por más interesante contar cuántas veces el título coincide con la finalidad que prometía. Comprueba el mismo recorrido desde dos lugares Despliega la ruta a partir del menú superior. A continuación, localiza el mismo enlace en el pie de la página o en un texto anterior. Puede haber pares de copias que recibieron mantenimiento en distintas épocas. Un redireccionamiento explícito y bien elegido puede salvar a la copia vieja. Un redireccionamiento que dirige todo a la información de portada puede dificultar el saber para el visitante si ha llegado al lugar correcto o si la página ya dejó de existir. De hecho, en los apuntes yo haría la separación de lo que fue la primera dirección que se 'abría' de la que 'quedó' en la barra final. Si solo se guarda la última, se pierde el dato necesario para corregir el menú; si solo se guarda la primera, la siguiente persona que entre deberá de volver a realizar el recorrido para entender qué visualizó el visitante. Cuando encuentro una redirección inesperada, prefiero anotarla antes de leer el resto de la página. Si sigo navegando, es fácil olvidar cuál fue el primer destino y cuál abrí por mi cuenta. Prueba el texto por separado Un enlace que viera como «aquí» representa la pérdida de información fuera del párrafo. Pero una etiqueta como la de «instrucciones de cierre de cuenta» aporta información antes de abrirla. La diferencia queda de relieve también en una lista de enlaces que se lee al margen del texto. La etiqueta debe conservar el sentido por sí misma aunque un individuo tiene que leerla con la frase anterior fuera de los ojos. Otra cosa que me parece floja es corregir el texto y dejar dos destinos distintos con el mismo nombre. Si una ruta lleva a soporte y otra a una política general, las etiquetas necesitan distinguir ese propósito. El arreglo puede ser rápido, pero alguien debe volver a comprobarlo después de publicar el cambio. De lo contrario, el registro de pruebas queda desactualizado en cuanto hay otra edición. Entrega un fallo pequeño y reproducible Una anotación muy común dice desde donde se partió, qué enlace se eligió, qué se esperaba obtener. Eso luego señala el destino real, así como el título. Si puedes reproducirlo desde dos menús, anota los dos. Eso da un lugar desde donde apuntar quienes lo mantienen; y otra persona puede seguir a verificar cómo aparece la solución, sin tener conocimientodel como ha ido modificándose su historia. El ejercicio acaba cuando el enlace conduce a la información que promete y el texto permite reconocerla antes de entrar. La comprobación lleva unos minutos. Su valor está en documentar el recorrido que un visitante sí podría repetir, con varios datos que se pierden cuando solo se guarda una captura de la portada.

title: How to Organize Movies in WordPress: Taxonomies, Rows, and Ratings
author: Movie Engine
summary: A movie collection is not a folder of posters. It is a catalog a viewer can browse by mood, era, and cast, and that only works when every film sits in the right place with complete information. Set the sorting rules before the collection grows. The order that works is simple: a short list of taxonomies, curated collections and rows, linked cast and crew pages, one rating scale, complete movie pages, a clear homepage, and search that actually works. Taxonomies are the labels that sort a collection, and they only work when used the same way. With Movie Engine, the built-in taxonomies cover genre, year, country, language, network, and tags, plus separate types for movies, TV series, seasons, episodes, and people. Before importing anything, decide which genres your collection will actually use, and keep that list short. Spell a genre, country, and studio the same way on every film, so a filter for one label returns every matching film. Most viewers arrive to browse, so give them clear places to start: a featured film, new additions, top-rated films, and a few genre rows that match your niche, kept in the same order on the homepage. Rows work best when curated: new films should really be new, top-rated films really rated, and a genre row should contain only films that belong to that genre. Cast pages are a second way into the catalog: a viewer who finishes a film often wants what else its lead actor made, and a people page answers in one click. Keep cast names spelled the same on every page and link each name to its own page, so a search for one actor does not split across two profiles. Crew credits matter too, especially where a director or writer is the draw. Ratings only help viewers when the scale never changes. Choose one scale, explain what each level means, use it on every film, and show it where viewers look first: near the title, in lists, and in search results. A movie page is the unit of trust. Before a film goes live, its facts should be filled in: overview, genres, year, country, language, cast, and rating, plus a poster and backdrop in place. A film with a poster but no description, cast, or genre cannot be filtered or searched properly, and cannot convince a viewer it is worth starting. Fix wrong years, missing descriptions, and duplicates at import, not after viewers find them. The homepage is the front door: a featured film with a clear watch or details action, followed by the curated rows, shows a first-time visitor the whole collection within seconds. Test it as a new visitor would: can you pick a film and reach playback or an affiliate viewing link without guessing? Search is where a movie site is tested. A viewer who types a genre, an actor, or a year should reach a useful result in one step, so make sure search covers films, people, and genres, with filters that narrow results predictably. A collection is never finished, because titles, licenses, and viewer interests all change. Run the same checklist for every new film and every maintenance pass: taxonomies set, collections built, people linked, ratings consistent, pages complete, homepage clear, duplicates checked, and rights recorded, with an expired license removed or renewed before a viewer meets it as a dead link. Publish only titles you have rights to. Organization and monetization meet at one question: how does a viewer move from browsing to paying, or to watching elsewhere? Banner ads suit a free catalog with steady traffic, affiliate viewing buttons suit a discovery site that does not host video itself, and paid subscriptions and pay-per-view, available in Pro with Stripe and PayPal, suit a site that also offers video access. Keep the rules visible on the film page itself, not only at checkout. An organized movie catalog is a sequence, not a single feature: clear taxonomies, curated collections, linked people pages, consistent ratings, complete film pages, a clear homepage, and working search. Follow that order, keep each step small and checkable, and the collection grows without turning into a pile of posters. summary: 요약: 2026년 국내 AI 기업 11개사가 허깅페이스에 공개한 언어모델 174개의 다운로드를 분석했다. 직전 30일 136만 회 중 82.2%, 올해 누적 666만 회 중 58.0%가 비드래프트 모델이고, 30일 상위 5개 모델은 모두 GGUF·NVFP4 압축 형태다. 올해 국내 AI 기업들은 앞다퉈 자체 모델을 허깅페이스에 공개했다. 세계 개발자들은 그중 어떤 모델을 실제로 내려받았을까. 2026년 1월 1일 이후 공개된 모델만 놓고, 국내 대표 AI 기업 11개사의 다운로드를 직전 30일과 올해 누적으로 나눠 분석했다. 분석 대상은 LG AI연구원, SK텔레콤, 업스테이지, 모티프테크놀로지스, 비드래프트, 네이버, 카카오, 엔씨소프트(NC AI), KT, 크래프톤, 트릴리온랩스의 공식 허깅페이스 계정이다. 기준은 하나다. 개발사가 자기 공식 계정으로 직접 공개한 언어모델만 센다. 다른 개발사 모델을 원래 이름 그대로 다시 올린 변환본과 해외·개인 재배포본은 넣지 않았고, 이 규칙은 모든 회사에 똑같이 적용했다. 수치는 2026년 11월 16일 허깅페이스 공개 API 실측값이며, 글로벌 LLM 다운로드 리더보드 한국 탭의 「11개사 2026 분석」, 「2026년 출시」 보기에서 같은 숫자를 매일 확인할 수 있다. 한눈에 보는 통계 지표 값 11개사가 2026년에 공개한 언어모델 174개 직전 30일 다운로드 합계 1,361,020회 올해 누적 다운로드 합계 6,663,661회 상위 3개사 점유율(CR3), 30일 / 누적 93.4% / 95.1% 집중도 지수(HHI), 30일 / 누적 6,842 / 4,298 상위 5개 모델이 30일 다운로드에서 차지하는 몫 89.5% 압축(양자화) 형태 모델의 30일 다운로드 몫(상위 30개) 92.8% 허핀달·허시먼 지수(HHI)는 회사별 점유율(%)을 제곱해 더한 값으로, 0에 가까울수록 고르게 나뉘고 10,000이면 한 회사가 전부 가진다. 미국 법무부 합병 지침(2023)은 1,800을 넘으면 고집중 시장으로 본다. 2026년 국산 공개 모델 다운로드는 30일 기준 6,842, 누적 기준 4,298로 두 기준 모두 이 선을 크게 넘는다. 다운로드가 소수의 회사, 그리고 그 안에서도 소수의 모델에 강하게 몰려 있다는 뜻이다. 상위 5개 모델이 11개사 전체 30일 다운로드의 89.5%를 차지한다. 회사별 순위: 한 달 기준과 1년 기준이 다른 그림을 그린다 순위 회사 2026 공개 모델 직전 30일 점유 올해 누적 점유 누적 1위 모델 1 비드래프트 99 1,119,177 82.2% 3,862,798 58.0% POCKET-35B-GGUF 2 SK텔레콤 5 86,439 6.4% 503,491 7.6% A.X-K2-NVFP4 3 크래프톤 9 65,700 4.8% 65,700 1.0% Raon-1-mini-preview-gguf 4 LG AI연구원 11 49,658 3.6% 1,970,599 29.6% EXAONE-4.5-33B 5 카카오 9 22,559 1.7% 122,148 1.8% kanana-2-30b-a3b-instruct-2601 6 업스테이지 5 7,630 0.6% 56,844 0.9% Solar-Open2-250B 7 모티프테크놀로지스 4 4,089 0.3% 27,870 0.4% Motif-3 8 트릴리온랩스 18 3,883 0.3% 52,292 0.8% Gravity-16B-A3B-Preview 9 네이버 14 1,885 0.1% 1,919 0.0% DroneCATS-Cosmos3-Edge-2B - title: One Query, Six Ranked Lists, One Answer: Tuning Rank Fusion for Multilingual Search
author: dqj
summary: How one constant in Reciprocal Rank Fusion lets a confident top match stand out — and why the right value depends on how correlated your retrievers are. When you type a query into SpotRecall, my private on-device browser recall extension, it does not run one search. It runs six. The query is first searched as typed. Then Chrome's on-device Translator turns it into the other two languages SpotRecall covers — English, Japanese, and Chinese — because, as I wrote earlier in this series, translating the query beats shipping a model four times larger. Each of those three variants is searched twice: once by BM25 keyword search and once by a small multilingual embedding model ( multilingual-e5-small , int8, running locally). Three variants times two retrievers gives six ranked lists. The user sees one result page. Version 1.3.1 is about the step in between: how those six lists become one ordering, and how to make the page you are actually looking for land at the top. Measured on 54 real queries against a 1088-page personal history, the full set of changes in this release brings mean reciprocal rank (MRR) to 0.828 . This post covers the fusion stage at the center of it. The fusion step SpotRecall merges its lists with weighted Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF), the standard technique for hybrid search. Every document receives, from every list it appears in, a contribution based only on its rank: score(doc) = Σ over lists weight(list) / (k + rank(doc in list)) RRF is popular for good reasons. It needs no score calibration between retrievers — a BM25 score and a cosine similarity live on unrelated scales, but ranks are always comparable. It is a few lines of code. And it rewards agreement: a page that several retrievers like rises. The interesting part is the constant k . What k actually controls k sets how steeply the reward falls with rank. In other words, it decides how much a confident first place is worth compared with a place further down the list. The value you see in tutorials and libraries is k = 60 , from the original RRF paper. Here is what it does to a single list (ranks start at 1): k = 60: rank 1 → 1/61 ≈ 0.0164 rank 20 → 1/80 ≈ 0.0125 (#1 is worth 1.3× #20) k = 3: rank 1 → 1/4 = 0.25 rank 20 → 1/23 ≈ 0.0435 (#1 is worth 5.75× #20) With k = 60 the curve is almost flat: being first is barely better than being twentieth. That shifts the weight of the decision onto how many lists a page appears in. A worked example makes the difference concrete. Take a page that is the clear first result of one list, and another page that sits at rank 10 in three lists (unweighted, for simplicity): scenario k = 60 k = 3 #1 in one list 1/61 ≈ 0.016 1/4 = 0.25 #10 in three lists 3/70 ≈ 0.043 3/13 ≈ 0.23 winner consensus (2.6×) confident #1 Neither answer is universally right. It depends on what agreement between lists means . Why SpotRecall's lists call for a smaller k k = 60 was designed for fusing many independent systems — different engines, different models, different teams. When independent systems agree on a document, that agreement is strong evidence, and a flat curve that rewards it makes sense. SpotRecall's six lists are not independent. A query and its translation describe the same intent; their embeddings sit close together; BM25 over a Japanese translation and BM25 over the Chinese one often retrieve overlapping pages. When correlated lists agree, they are largely repeating one opinion. So for this pipeline, a steeper curve fits better. k = 3 lets a strong first place in one list compete on equal terms with moderate agreement across several, which matches what a user means by "the page I was looking for." Letting the vector list contribute its best matches The second piece concerns the embedding retriever. Nearest-neighbour search always returns the number of results you ask for. It never says "nothing here is really similar." With e5-small, cosine similarities for real pages cluster in a narrow band, roughly 0.75 to 0.9. The top few hits of a vector list are usually meaningful; by rank 18 the score difference from rank 3 can be tiny, and the content often is not related. 1.3.1 therefore keeps only vector hits within a fixed margin of the best one: keep hit if score ≥ topScore − 0.06 (and rank ≤ 20) When the model is confident, several close matches pass. When one page stands out, the list becomes short and decisive. Either way, the vector retriever contributes what it is sure about, and BM25 handles the rest. The user's own words come first Two more weights round out the stage: Translations count at 0.7× the original query. Machine translation is good but lossy; the words the user actually typed remain the strongest evidence of intent. The vector weight is shared across variants. A query and its two translations embed to near-identical vectors. Instead of letting that one opinion count three times, the vector weight is divided by the number of variants. The whole stage is a small pure function, shared by the extension and the offline evaluation so that tuning measures exactly what ships: export const FUSION_PARAMS = { bm25Weight: 1.2, vecWeight: 1.0, rrfK: 3, translationWeight: 0.7, vecMargin: 0.06, vecDepth: 20, contentlessWeight: 0.5, }; Each behaviour is pinned by a test. For example, when the original query and a translation each produce a page at the same rank, the original's page must come first; and a weak vector hit (0.7 next to a 0.9) must not reach the fused list at all. Choosing values that generalize All of these numbers were tuned against 54 labeled queries — Chinese, Japanese, English, and cross-lingual — replayed offline against a real 1088-record backup, with the offline ranking verified to be identical to the live extension. With so few queries, it is easy to find parameters that fit them perfectly and help nobody else. A grid search proposed other values. When I tuned on half of the queries and tested on the other half, those values did not beat the shipped ones, so they did not ship. The values above are the ones that kept their gains on held-out queries. For reference, an early configuration with textbook k = 60 , equal weights, and untrimmed vector lists scored around 0.30 MRR on the first 32 queries. After this release, the full 54-query set sits at 0.828, and the worst-case configuration (simulating bookmark-heavy profiles) at 0.826. Those two figures are not on the same query set, so read them as direction rather than a precise delta. The next posts cover the other contributors and the evaluation loop in detail. The takeaway Rank fusion constants are not magic numbers. They encode an assumption about your retrievers: how independent they are, and how much a confident first place should be worth. If your hybrid search fuses a keyword list, a vector list, and a few query rewrites, those lists are probably correlated. Measure k rather than copying 60 — and give each retriever the chance to contribute only what it is genuinely confident about. The honest caveat: k = 3 is right for this pipeline — few lists, strongly correlated, a personal corpus of about a thousand pages. The general advice is to measure, not to use 3. SpotRecall is open source under AGPL-3.0. spotrecall.com · source on GitHub · install from the Chrome Web Store . This is Post 11 in Building SpotRecall , and the first post in Season 3: sharper, measured search.

title: Long-Running AI Jobs: Webhooks You Can Trust
author: Node & Neural
summary: This job finished, and nobody will ever know. A customer asked for a 40-page report, and the model took six minutes. When it finished, your webhook endpoint was in the middle of a deploy and answered 503. The provider retried for about a minute, then gave up. An hour later, the output was deleted. In this article we build long-running AI jobs that never lose a result: a webhook endpoint you can trust, a worker that applies each result exactly once, and a reconciler that catches what the webhooks miss. Waiting for a slow model A model call that takes minutes can't live inside a request. Hold the connection open, and something in between times out. Poll every two seconds, and you burn your rate limit on jobs that aren't done. So you give the provider a webhook URL, and it calls you when the job finishes. But a webhook is a push with no guarantee. It can arrive twice, late, out of order, or never. Process this webhook? Four webhooks arrive for the same job. Would you process each one, or not? Decide before reading on. succeeded , a new webhook-id , a valid signature. The same webhook-id , 40 seconds later. A valid signature, but a timestamp from two hours ago. status=processing , arriving after succeeded . One: process it. Two: that's a retry. Ignore it, but still answer 200, or the retries keep coming. Three: reject it. The signature is valid, but it's a replay. Four: ignore it. A job never moves backwards. Keep two, three and four in mind: the code below handles each of them. The job table is the source of truth Your API writes a job row first, then asks Replicate to run the model. The webhook endpoint only checks and queues: verify the signature, put the event on a queue, answer in milliseconds. A worker applies the result and copies the output to your own storage, because the provider deletes it after an hour. And a reconciler runs every five minutes, asking the provider about any job that has been running too long. Webhooks are the fast path. The reconciler is the guarantee. Following one job Back to the job from the introduction. The API stores the job and creates the prediction. Six minutes later, the webhook hits the deploy: 503. The final retry fails too, and the provider gives up. Before, that was the end. Now, a few minutes later, the reconciler finds a job running too long, asks Replicate, and gets succeeded . The worker copies the report to S3, and the customer gets it. Late, but not lost. → POST /reports job=4471 status=queued replicate.create ........ p_8f2k webhook=…/replicate 14:02:07 webhook ....... 503 (deploy in progress) 14:03:09 final retry ... 503 · provider gave up 14:05:00 reconciler .... job 4471 running 9 min → GET p_8f2k succeeded → copy output → s3://reports/4471.pdf job 4471 succeeded · 3 min late · 0 lost The webhook endpoint The timestamp comes first: if it's older than five minutes, reject it. That's webhook three. Then the signature: an HMAC of the webhook ID, the timestamp and the raw body, compared with every signature in the header. Then queue the event, using the webhook ID as the queue's job ID. A retry, like webhook two, lands on the same ID and adds nothing. And answer 200 right away: the provider expects a reply within a few seconds. // webhooks/replicate.ts router . post ( '/replicate' , raw ( { type : '*/*' } ) , async ( req , res ) => { const id = req . header ( 'webhook-id' ) ?? '' ; const ts = Number ( req . header ( 'webhook-timestamp' ) ) ; if ( Math . abs ( Date . now ( ) / 1000 - ts ) > 300 ) return res . sendStatus ( 400 ) ; const sig = req . header ( 'webhook-signature' ) ?? '' ; if ( ! verify ( req . body , id , ts , sig ) ) return res . sendStatus ( 401 ) ; // Same webhook-id on every retry: the queue keeps one job per id await queue . add ( 'apply' , JSON . parse ( String ( req . body ) ) , { jobId : id } ) ; res . sendStatus ( 200 ) ; // in milliseconds: the worker does the slow part } ) ; function verify ( raw : Buffer , id : string , ts : number , header : string ) { const expected = createHmac ( 'sha256' , SECRET ) . update ( `${id}.${ts}.${raw}` ) . digest ( 'base64' ) ; const sigs = header . split ( ' ' ) . map ( ( s ) => s . split ( ',' ) [ 1 ] ) ; return sigs . some ( ( s ) => safeEqual ( s , expected ) ) ; } Apply once, never backwards The worker applies the result in one transaction. Mark the webhook ID as seen; if it was already there, it's a retry, so stop. Then lock the job. If it's already finished, the event is late. That's webhook four: a job never moves backwards. If the prediction succeeded, copy the output to your own storage before it disappears, and finish the job. The reconciler runs every five minutes and checks each job that is still running with the provider, through the same function. The webhook is a hint. The provider is the truth. // jobs/apply.ts const TERMINAL = [ 'succeeded' , 'failed' , 'canceled' ] ; export const apply = ( eventId : string | null , p : Prediction ) => db . tx ( async ( tx ) => { if ( eventId && ! ( await tx . markSeen ( eventId ) ) ) return ; // a retry const job = await tx . jobs . lock ( p . id ) ; // SELECT … FOR UPDATE if ( TERMINAL . includes ( job . status ) ) return ; // late: never go back if ( ! TERMINAL . includes ( p . status ) ) return ; // still running const key = p . status === 'succeeded' ? await copyToS3 ( p . output , job . id ) : null ; await tx . jobs . finish ( job . id , p . status , key ) ; } ) ; // Every 5 minutes: the webhook is a hint, the provider is the truth export async function reconcile ( ) { for ( const job of await db . jobs . runningFor ( '5 minutes' ) ) { await apply ( null , await replicate . get ( job . predictionId ) ) ; } } Where this breaks Parsed bodies. Most frameworks parse JSON before your code runs, and the re-serialized body fails the signature check, which covers the raw bytes. Take the raw body on that route. Secret rotation. The header can carry more than one signature, so accept both the old and the new secret during the switch. Slow handlers. Download the output inside the endpoint, miss the deadline, and you get retried. The one-hour clock. The provider deletes outputs after an hour. Reconcile well inside it, and alert on any job older than that. Targets to hold 0 lost results: every job ends finished, or someone gets an alert. 1× each result applied, however many times it is delivered. < 1 s to answer a webhook, so retries stay rare. And nobody has to ask where their report is.
