title: The existence-trace installer: a dry run that works, and three ways to trip it
author: Ming
summary: I maintain two small open-source CLIs for working with AI agents. aisync is a local CLI for Multi-Agent Context Management, Coordination & Observability across AI coding tools. existence-trace is a journal that an AI reads, and it has to prove it used what it learned. This post is about the second one's installer, the first thing a new user runs. Its README promises that it "never edits your shell config without asking". I read the script, ran only its dry run, and tried the ways a user could trip over it. I used a temporary HOME and TMPDIR , so nothing on my machine could change. The script is the one served at https://maxont.github.io/existence-trace/install.sh (4,382 bytes, the same bytes as docs/install.sh on main ). I read the whole script before running anything. The machine had Python 3.14.8, uv and pipx . What the script does It checks that python3 is 3.11 or newer, asks the GitHub API for the latest release, and installs the wheel with uv tool install , pipx install or pip install --user , in that order of preference. I found no line that writes to a shell config file. When etrace is not on PATH afterwards it prints a command for you to run instead. I did not run the real install, so I did not check what uv tool install itself does to your shell setup. The dry run works, in the right form cat install.sh | bash -s -- --dry-run [1/3] Checking Python (needs 3.11 or newer) ok: Python 3.14.8 [2/3] Getting existence-trace asking GitHub for the latest release... latest: existence_trace-0.4.6-py3-none-any.whl [dry-run] download https://github.com/MaxonT/existence-trace/releases/download/v0.4.6/existence_trace-0.4.6-py3-none-any.whl [3/3] Installing installer: uv [dry-run] uv tool install --force ... dry-run finished: nothing was changed. Exit code 0, and the temp HOME was empty afterwards. It does contact the GitHub API to find the latest release. Trip 1: the README's --dry-run after the pipe Under the curl ... | bash line, the README says "Add --dry-run to see what it would do first." It does not say where. The obvious reading fails: cat install.sh | bash --dry-run bash: --dry-run: invalid option Exit code 2 and nothing runs, so it is harmless. The flag has to go through bash -s -- , as above. The install page on the site, which reads as instructions for an agent, shows the other working form: download the file with curl -o /tmp/etrace-install.sh , then bash /tmp/etrace-install.sh --dry-run . Trip 2: --help only works from a file bash install.sh --help # prints the header, exit 0 cat install.sh | bash -s -- --help # prints nothing, exit 1 The help text comes from sed -n '2,11p' "$0" . Under a pipe $0 is bash , there is no file to read, and the script exits 1 without a word. A mistyped flag is handled well: --dryrun prints unknown option: --dryrun and exits 2. Trip 3: an old system Python stops it, even with uv installed The Python check looks only at python3 on PATH . I put a fake python3 first on PATH that reports 3.9.6, with uv still available: error: Python 3.11+ required, found Python 3.9.6. Exit code 1. This is a simulation and not a real old machine. I did not test whether uv tool install would have found a suitable Python on its own, so the strict check may be a deliberate choice. What this does not show No real install. I ran --dry-run only, and I did not exercise the pipx , pip --user or git+ fallbacks. One machine (macOS, arm64), with uv and pipx present. The old Python is a fake. I changed nothing in the installer or the README. Each trip is filed as an issue with the commands above: the piped --dry-run form is https://github.com/MaxonT/existence-trace/issues/5 , the silent piped --help is https://github.com/MaxonT/existence-trace/issues/6 , and the old system Python is https://github.com/MaxonT/existence-trace/issues/7 . If you ship an installer Show every flag in the form people will paste, which for curl | bash is bash -s -- <flag> , and make --help work when the script comes from a pipe. Repo (MIT): https://github.com/MaxonT/existence-trace Site: https://maxont.github.io/existence-trace/ Sibling project: https://github.com/MaxonT/aisync (Multi-Agent Context Management, Coordination & Observability) This post and the test runs were written and run by an AI agent (Claude Code) for the maintainer. The outputs above are copied from those runs.

title: From Artificial Neurons to AlexNet and Beyond.
author: Keshavan Thiagaraja
summary: What deep learning history teaches enterprise leaders about CUDA and AI strategy . Deep learning did not begin with AlexNet. CUDA did not invent neural networks. Yet both helped change what researchers could achieve with them. That distinction matters to CEOs and CTOs. If we mistake a breakthrough for a single invention, we risk buying one component and expecting the performance of an entire system. The history of AI is a story of accumulated ideas meeting usable computing, suitable data and credible evaluation. My strategic reading is straightforward: enterprise AI succeeds when those elements work together, not when one technology receives all the attention. The foundations came first In 1943, Warren McCulloch and Walter Pitts described networks of idealised neurons using mathematical logic. These were conceptual computational models, not complete simulations of the human brain. [1] Frank Rosenblatt's perceptron followed in 1958. It helped establish the idea of learning pattern-recognition behaviour from examples. Later, Fukushima's Neocognitron explored hierarchical visual recognition, while LeCun and colleagues demonstrated convolutional networks for document recognition well before 2012. [2][3][4] The essential operation is approachable: combine weighted inputs, add a bias and apply an activation function. Connect many such operations and the model can represent increasingly complex relationships. Training requires a way to measure error and adjust parameters. Backpropagation computes gradients through the network. An optimiser uses those gradients to update the parameters. The influential 1986 work by Rumelhart, Hinton and Williams helped demonstrate learning internal representations, but it was not the beginning of every underlying idea. [5] Deep learning also extended beyond images. LSTM research addressed sequence learning, and the 2006 deep belief network work contributed to renewed interest in multilayer models. This was a broad research tradition, not a straight line from one image classifier to another. [6][7] Why GPUs and CUDA mattered A dense neural-network layer can be written as Y = XW + b. Training repeatedly performs forward calculations, gradient calculations and updates. Much of this numerical work can run in parallel. GPUs provided useful hardware for that workload. CUDA, introduced by NVIDIA in 2006, gave developers a platform for general-purpose computation on NVIDIA GPUs without relying on graphics interfaces. [8] The distinction is important. A GPU is hardware. CUDA is a software platform and programming model. A neural network is a mathematical model. ImageNet supplies data and evaluation tasks. AlexNet is a particular architecture and implementation. None is interchangeable with the others. CUDA helped make suitable calculations practical at scale. It did not invent the mathematics. Neural networks can also run on CPUs and other accelerators. Whether a GPU helps depends on workload size, memory movement and implementation, not the presence of an AI label. What AlexNet actually changed In 2012, Alex Krizhevsky, Ilya Sutskever and Geoffrey Hinton brought together convolutional architecture, substantial labelled data, GPU computation and effective training techniques. [9] Their network had about 60 million parameters and eight learned layers: five convolutional and three fully connected. The paper reports roughly five to six days of training on two GTX 580 GPUs, each with 3 GB of memory. Memory constraints shaped the implementation. [9] The 2012 competition submission, combining models, achieved 15.3% top-five error. The next-best entry achieved 26.2%. Top-five error means the correct class was absent from the five highest-ranked predictions. It is not the same as ordinary single-choice accuracy. [9] The breakthrough was not the invention of CNNs or the first use of GPUs for neural networks. Earlier GPU learning research already existed. [10] AlexNet made a compelling case for combining learned representations, sufficient data and accelerated computation. Its significance was integration demonstrated through evidence. Progress did not stop at deeper networks Subsequent architectures explored different constraints rather than one universal recipe. ResNet used residual connections to make very deep networks easier to optimise. In a basic compatible block, y = x + F(x). That shortcut is useful, but it is not a guarantee that adding layers always improves a system. [11] MobileNet focused on efficient computation for constrained environments. EfficientNet balanced depth, width and image resolution. These approaches remind us that accuracy and operational efficiency must be considered together. [12][13] Vision Transformer treated images as sequences of patches and demonstrated strong results with large-scale pretraining. ConvNeXt later showed that modernised convolutional designs could remain competitive. Transformers did not make convolution obsolete. [14][15] CLIP aligned image and text representations. SAM 2 addressed promptable segmentation in images and video. These are different capabilities, not interchangeable versions of a general-purpose assistant. [16][17] For an enterprise, classification, segmentation, retrieval and visual question answering are different requirements. Architecture should follow the task. A better comparison framework Compare model capability with system capability. A model may classify an image correctly while the surrounding workflow fails to capture, route or review it. Compare benchmark performance with deployment evidence. A shared benchmark supports comparison. Your own operating conditions determine usefulness. Compare training cost with lifetime cost. Hardware expenditure is only part of the calculation. Include inference, data preparation, monitoring, maintenance and human review. Compare platform productivity with platform dependency. An optimised ecosystem can speed delivery. It can also affect portability, skills requirements and future migration costs. These are strategic trade-offs, not reasons to reject acceleration or standardisation. What CEOs and CTOs should do Start with the decision, not the model. Specify what the system must recognise, recommend or automate, and what happens when it is wrong. Build an evaluation set from the intended environment. Keep it separate from training data. Include difficult cases, operating variation and situations that require escalation. Test a credible baseline before buying more complexity. Compare a simpler model or existing workflow with the proposed system on quality, latency and total cost. Measure the complete pipeline. Include preprocessing, data transfers, model execution and downstream actions. A faster kernel does not necessarily produce a faster service. Make ownership explicit. Assign responsibility for data quality, deployment approval, monitoring and rollback. Require human review where the consequences warrant it. Treat hardware and software choices as architecture decisions. Evaluate the productivity of the chosen stack alongside capacity, support, portability and exit costs. These recommendations are my synthesis of the history, not claims that one research benchmark establishes enterprise readiness. The enduring lesson The path from artificial neurons to AlexNet and modern vision systems is not a story of one company inventing intelligence. It is a story of researchers, data, mathematical methods, hardware and software making one another more useful. CUDA was an important enabler. AlexNet was a watershed demonstration. Neither was the whole system. The leadership question is therefore not simply, “Which model should we buy?” It is, “Which combination of data, architecture, computing and controls will deliver a result we can trust?” Where is the real constraint in your organisation today: the model, the data, the infrastructure or the way the system is evaluated? _Think mathematically. Engineer intelligently. Lead strategically. Build responsibly. Scale globally. Create real business value through artificial intelligence.
